evidence_level_values.branded-rct: Branded ingredient with own RCTs (0.9x multiplier) - e.g., KSM-66, Meriva

study_type_values.systematic_review_meta: Meta-analysis or systematic review (6 base pts)
study_type_values.clinical_strain: Probiotic strain clinical evidence (4 base pts)

_metadata._scoring_formula: score = study_type_base_points × evidence_level_multiplier (computed live by scorer, not stored)

_scoring_fields_used.study_type: Determines base points: systematic_review_meta=6, rct_multiple=5, rct_single=4, clinical_strain=4, observational=2, animal_study=2, in_vitro=1
_scoring_fields_used.evidence_level: Determines multiplier: product-human=1.0, branded-rct=0.9, ingredient-human=0.9, strain-clinical=0.65, preclinical=0.3
_scoring_fields_used.score_contribution: Metadata label (tier_1/tier_2/tier_3) reflecting computed score bracket. Not used by scorer.

backed_clinical_studies.effect_direction_rationale: One six-week symptom-endpoint RCT supports this complete formula for adult bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort. Attrition (350 baseline; 219 at week six), sponsor involvement and lack of independent symptom-endpoint replication limit certainty. Two related small mechanistic publications under a shared protocol do not establish additional clinical benefits or independent symptom replication.
key_endpoints: Self-reported bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort
backed_clinical_studies.notes: Evidence is for the whole 24-strain plus pomegranate formulation, not individual strains, skin, heart health or micronutrient synthesis. 350 is the baseline sample of the symptom trial, not a sum across studies. No CFU conversion is known or used. PMID 40944126 and 41750436 share protocol NCT04171466; both report 32 randomized, with 27 and 21 completing respectively. The registration reports 46 actual participants across four arms; unique cohort overlap is unresolved, so counts are not summed. Their microbiome/metabolite and barrier outcomes are not independent symptom replication or demonstrated prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Trial reports establish the named formula, strain list and total potency, not the commercial label's per-blend or individual-strain quantities. Commercial per-blend allocations remain label-identity constraints only. The signed A032 limited whole-formula decision, accepted by Dr. Pham on 2026-10-26 as attested by Sean, is now encoded for the six-week symptom trial only. Its initial three-day titration is not copied into the separate 91-day mechanistic regimens. Existing exact formula matching remains required; native AFU is not converted to CFU and individual strain effects are not inferred.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: REVIEWED DISEASE-CONTEXT RESEARCH, NON-SCORING. The cited studies concern oral Meriva preparation in osteoarthritis, adjunct psoriasis treatment, and biopsy-confirmed NASH. Their findings do not establish the former stress/anxiety, muscle-recovery, or longevity tags. Osteoarthritis: an open controlled registry, 100 participants, 1 g Meriva/day (200 mg total curcuminoids), eight months. Psoriasis: 63 participants, 2 g Meriva/day as an adjunct to topical corticosteroids, 12 weeks. NASH: 52 participants, 2 g Meriva/day, 72 weeks. These are studied regimens, not newly imposed efficacy thresholds. Keep preparation mass distinct from total curcuminoids and pure curcumin. Existing reference-only handling retains this research while avoiding numerical efficacy outside established applicability. No clinician sign-off or universal lack-of-efficacy conclusion is asserted.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence exists but is endpoint-, population-, form-, and dose-specific. A seven-RCT meta-analysis reported less post-exercise soreness and short-lived improvement in muscle-damage markers, especially in resistance-training and untrained groups. A 37-RCT meta-analysis reported a modest average body-weight effect, strongest in adults with overweight or obesity and around 2 g/day. A separate systematic review of prolonged use in healthy adults found effects only under specific conditions and raised unresolved long-term TMAO questions. This record is not broad proof of energy, cardiovascular, fat-burning, or athletic-performance efficacy.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 32154768 pooled seven randomized trials of exercise-induced muscle damage and reported improvements in soreness and some 24-hour biomarkers, while calling for further research. PMID 32359762 pooled 37 randomized trials (2,292 participants) and found modest weight and BMI changes, particularly in adults with overweight or obesity; its dose-response analysis suggested the largest body-weight effect near 2 g/day. PMID 32958033 reviewed 11 prolonged-supplementation studies in healthy adults using 1-4 g/day for 12-24 weeks and concluded that physical-performance effects occur only in specific conditions.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence supports NAC as a glutathione precursor that measurably lowers oxidative-stress markers, and a randomized trial supports attenuation of influenza-like illness in older adults. Respiratory (mucolytic) and psychiatric-adjunct evidence is real but condition-specific and more heterogeneous. Signed A094 accepts limited oral exercise-soreness findings only. The exercise research is retained as nonaffirmative reference for those currentcatalog purposes.24h soreness benefit is separate from immediate null and adverse functional-recovery findings;less soreness isnot proven bettertrainingadaptation. No universalNACdosecurve or blanketinefficacy conclusion is created.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A 6-month randomized, double-blind, 20-centre trial (PMID 9230243, n=262, NAC 600 mg twice daily, 78% aged 65+) significantly reduced the frequency and severity of influenza-like episodes and shifted cell-mediated immunity from anergy toward normoergy; notably it did not prevent A/H1N1 infection, but only 25% of infected participants on NAC developed symptomatic illness versus 79% on placebo. A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 20 supplementation studies (PMID 39632267) found significantly increased glutathione and reduced TBARS and IL-6, with no significant effect on TNF-alpha, creatine kinase or GSSG. A major review of mucolytic agents in chronic bronchitis/COPD (PMID 31107966) supports benefit in respiratory settings, and a 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis (PMID 29457216) found psychiatric-adjunct evidence that is promising but heterogeneous across diagnoses.

purpose_evidence.rationale: Cardiovascular outcome evidence is mixed across reviews and trials. PMID 31567003 reports studied doses of 376-4000 mg/day; 376 mg is the lowest included exposure, not a demonstrated efficacy cutoff. EFSA identifies 2-4 g/day EPA+DHA for maintenance of triglyceride levels. PMID 37264945 supports a dose-responsive triglyceride effect, more evident above 2 g/day in hyperlipidemia/overweight populations. PMID 31422671 concerns prescription therapy at 4 g/day and does not establish OTC equivalence or a 2 g treatment guarantee. The updated Cochrane review PMID 32114706 finds high-certainty triglyceride reduction and at most small, outcome-specific coronary benefits; this does not establish universal cardiovascular protection. Full-credit thresholds and interpolation belong to quality_score.json.

PMID 18184094 recommends an average daily intake of at least 200 mg DHA for pregnant and lactating women. This is total intake guidance, not proof of preterm-birth prevention from a 200 mg supplement. Numerical credit is editorial policy in quality_score.json.

Secondary outcomes (URTI, LRTI, ARI hospital admission or emergency attendance, antimicrobial courses, work/school absence): no statistically significant effect overall (Table 4).
At least one serious adverse event: adjusted OR 0.98 (0.80 to 1.20), P=0.83.

limitations: Severe baseline deficiency and dosing schedule modified findings; most infections were not microbiologically confirmed.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient: NIH ODS documents its requirement for central nervous system development, myelination and function, healthy red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis, with RDAs of 2.4 to 2.8 mcg for adults. Nutritional adequacy is a DRI-authority assessment owned by the dose and nutrition path (rda_optimal_uls.json, nutrition_authority_floor), not by this registry. The one interventional synthesis held here answers a narrower question - cognitive function, depressive symptoms and idiopathic fatigue in people WITHOUT overt B12 deficiency or advanced neurological disorders - and found no effect. That null is not evidence about vitamin B12 generally.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 33809274 (Nutrients 2021) pooled 16 RCTs and 6,276 participants in 'patients without advanced neurological disorders or overt vitamin B12 deficiency' and found no evidence for an effect of B12 alone or B-complex supplementation on any subdomain of cognitive function and no overall effect on measures of depression; only one study reported idiopathic fatigue, so no fatigue analysis was possible. The NIH ODS Vitamin B12 Health Professional fact sheet documents essentiality, deficiency and recommended intakes. Scope repair 2026-09-18: that null previously carried an ingredient-human effect direction across every B12-containing product; the entry is now a reference-tier anchor and describes only the question its source answered.

backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: The Cochrane review, updated November 2023 (PMID 37947276, fifth update; 50 RCTs, 8857 randomised participants), found in moderate-certainty evidence that cranberry products reduce the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (RR 0.70) — in women with recurrent UTIs, in children and in people susceptible after an intervention — with little or no benefit in institutionalised elderly people, pregnant women or people with neuromuscular bladder dysfunction; one trial compared tablets with liquid and two compared PAC doses, so equivalence of preparations and PAC doses stays uncertain. PMID 35833477 evaluates chicory-derived preparations: 3–20 g/day, 50 studies/2525 participants, with bowel-function benefits in healthy subjects and no significant bifidogenic benefit in the gastrointestinal-disorder subgroup. Live bibliographic metadata for PMID 35833477 lists BENEO support and author affiliations; precise funder roles require full-text review. PMID 38309832 reports small cardiometabolic risk-factor effects with low or very low certainty, not cardiovascular-event prevention. Review populations overlap and must not be summed as unique enrollment. The strongest modern trials are on the standardized GutGard extract for functional dyspepsia, H. pylori management, and reflux-related symptoms, while older classic DGL ulcer trials were mixed or negative (PMID 21747893, PMID 23606875, PMID 39929150, PMID 4933135). Retained-source scope and limitations: No advantage over placebo in a 47-person DGL duodenal-ulcer trial (PMID: 4933135) Preparation-specific GutGard dyspepsia symptoms, H. pylori test outcomes and reflux symptoms; not proof of generic ulcer healing (PMID: 21747893; 23606875; 39929150)
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: GutGard placebo-controlled trials showed symptom improvement in functional dyspepsia (PMID 21747893), higher H. pylori clearance than placebo in a 60-day study (PMID 23606875), and faster relief of reflux-related symptoms in a larger 2025 trial (PMID 39929150). By contrast, a classic randomized DGL duodenal-ulcer trial found no advantage over placebo (PMID 4933135), so this entry should stay evidence-cautious.

backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A multicenter randomized trial in gastric-ulcer patients found polaprezinc comparable to rebamipide after 8 weeks, with endoscopic healing rates of 81.5% versus 74.3% (PMID 35999163). backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence concerns Boswellia serrata extracts for osteoarthritis pain, stiffness and function, not stress, longevity or broad immune benefit. This family-level association does not establish that an unspecified resin extract equals Aflapin or Boswellin Super in standardized composition, dose or onset. Enrollment 545 is the seven-trial 2020 review only; participants from the newer trials are not summed. No generic extract-mass threshold is established here. The former UNII X7B7P649WQ identifies BOSWELLIA SERRATA WHOLE, not an extract, and is not used as an extract identifier. Real-label review (2026-09-05) added the printed extract spellings gum extract, standardized extract, Apres-Flex, Casperome and frankincense phytosome as family-level extract preparations; a bare Boswellia serrata row with only a boswellic-acid form stays unmatched until its source states an extract. The primary outcome uses the locked vocabulary label Joint & Bone Health for osteoarthritis pain, stiffness and function.

Additional meta-analytic support exists in vascular dementia and MCI populations (PMID 24639880; PMID 30989926), but the evidence base remains quality-limited.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence for chromium picolinate is mixed but clearly beyond preclinical status. Meta-analyses in type 2 diabetes show statistically significant glycemic improvements on average, yet heterogeneity is high and at-risk or prediabetic populations often do not benefit in better-controlled trials (PMID 32730903, PMID 20634174, PMID 17519436).
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A 2020 meta-analysis of 28 randomized trials in type 2 diabetes reported reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, insulin, and HOMA-IR with chromium supplementation (PMID 32730903). However, a placebo-controlled trial in adults at risk for diabetes found no improvement in glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity with 500-1000 mcg/day chromium picolinate (PMID 20634174). Older systematic evidence also found more consistent benefit in diabetes than in non-diabetic populations, while highlighting study-quality concerns (PMID 17519436).

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Resveratrol has a broad human trial base, but the overall evidence remains mixed and outcome-specific. Some meta-analyses find modest improvements in inflammatory or lipid biomarkers, while others show no consistent clinically meaningful effect, so longevity-style claims remain substantially ahead of the data (PMID 39872318, PMID 35905799, PMID 39255906, PMID 29305228). Retained-source scope and limitations: Mixed inflammatory/lipid biomarker syntheses in selected patient groups; retained sources do not establish human longevity benefit (PMID: 39872318; 35905799; 39255906; 29305228)
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: Recent meta-analyses report reduced inflammatory and oxidative-stress biomarkers in type 2 diabetes (PMID 39872318) and lower CRP/TNF-alpha in cardiovascular populations (PMID 35905799). Lipid findings are inconsistent: some meta-analyses report dose-dependent LDL/TG reductions (PMID 36145131; PMID 39255906), whereas others find no meaningful lipid benefit overall (PMID 29305228; PMID 24111838).

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Curcumin has one of the largest human supplement trial literatures, with broad meta-analytic support for inflammatory, osteoarthritis, and some metabolic endpoints. However, formulation quality and bioavailability matter materially, and the strongest effects are generally seen with enhanced-delivery products rather than unformulated spice-level curcumin (PMID 39478418, PMID 38945354, PMID 38576215, PMID 40615851).
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A comprehensive 103-trial meta-analysis found high-credibility evidence for improvements in fasting glucose, CRP, HDL, and body weight, with significant effects across 23 of 42 pooled outcomes (PMID 39478418). Additional umbrella-style work supports anti-inflammatory and endothelial-function biomarker effects (PMID 38945354) and osteoarthritis symptom benefit (PMID 38576215), while newer disease-specific syntheses continue to show reductions in CRP and TNF-alpha in knee osteoarthritis (PMID 40615851).

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence for berberine is strong in metabolic-health settings, especially for glycemic control and selected lipid outcomes, but much of the literature is short-term, China-centered, and methodologically uneven. The overall signal is still clearly beyond preclinical status (PMID 34956436, PMID 37598753, PMID 36467075, PMID 36941490).
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: Meta-analyses in type 2 diabetes report significant reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, insulin resistance, and several lipid markers with berberine (PMID 34956436; PMID 36467075). Separate pooled analyses also show modest improvements in glycemic and insulin-related traits (PMID 37598753) and dyslipidemia endpoints (PMID 36941490). The evidence is favorable overall, but most trials remain short and geographically concentrated.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: The cited evidence includes different preparations and outcomes. PMID 36558392 tested MagteinPS, a combination of magnesium L-threonate, phosphatidylserine, vitamins C and D, and vitamin B6, not isolated Magtein. PMID 41601871 found benefits on selected cognition and subjective sleep-related impairment outcomes, but no between-group differences in objective sleep outcomes or several other sleep measures. The 21-day sleep trial is PMID 39252819; PMID 40567408 is its linked corrigendum, not an independent trial. backed_clinical_studies.notes: Both indexed randomized trials explicitly used Sunfiber PHGG supplied by Taiyo Kagaku; the evidence is for that ingredient preparation, not for a complete Nature's Way retail formula. Niv 2016 found selective improvement in bloating/gas, but not overall IBS severity, abdominal pain, stool frequency or quality of life; 121 randomized and 108 entered the reported intention-to-treat analysis, with substantial differential attrition. Yasukawa 2019 studied healthy adults with loose stools, excluding diagnosed IBS; 44 randomized, 42 stool-efficacy and 40 microbiome analyses. Stool form improved but frequency, GI symptom journals and overall physical/mental quality-of-life summaries did not. Microbiome composition is secondary surrogate evidence; neither indexed trial measured clinical immune benefits or increased SCFA production. The 2016 study received commercial support from Pro Natura and Sunwic AB with declared investigator independence. Taiyo funded and supplied the 2019 study, participated in protocol preparation and employed three authors; these are not independently funded replications. These limitations support the reviewed mixed clinical determination under the existing grading policy.

Retained-source scope and limitations: Blood-pressure findings depend on population and heterogeneity; no source-derived dose-response relationship established (PMID: 41000008) Migraine studies require route separation between intravenous acute treatment and oral prophylaxis; not retained sleep efficacy evidence (PMID: 26752497; 8792038)
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: NIH ODS Magnesium identifies hypertension, migraine, and low intake as the main clinically relevant contexts for supplementation. A recent blood-pressure meta-analysis found reductions of about 2.8/2.0 mm Hg overall, with larger effects in hypertensive or hypomagnesemic participants (PMID 41000008). For migraine, oral/intravenous magnesium meta-analysis and classic oral prophylaxis data support benefit in at least some patients (PMID 26752497; PMID 8792038).

Scope repair 2026-09-18: study_type was 'observational' although the source is a randomized controlled trial, and total_enrollment was 30 rather than the 19 the source states. The entry is now held at reference tier - it earns no evidence points - because one small off-axis null trial does not establish ingredient-level efficacy for the bone, joint and multivitamin uses these products carry boron for. Calcium fructoborate was removed from the aliases and excluded in applicability: it is a different compound with its own positive short-term trials, and merging the two materials let a plain-boron null speak for fructoborate products and vice versa. No source on this entry studied bone turnover, joint or inflammatory endpoints, so those key_endpoints were removed.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 8508192: 'The effect of boron supplementation on lean body mass, plasma testosterone levels, and strength in male bodybuilders' - 19 men, 2.5 mg/day for 7 weeks; plasma boron rose but 'analysis of variance indicated no significant effect of boron supplementation on any of the dependent variables'. PMID 7889885 is the same trial reported in Environmental Health Perspectives ('boron supplementation affects these variables not at all'). Calcium fructoborate trials - CRP, IL-6 and lipid markers over 30 days, and knee discomfort over 14 days - are a separate material and are deliberately not curated here; their identifiers are recorded in scripts/audits/evidence_expansion_2026_09/NULL_SCOPE_AUDIT.md rather than on this entry, and a calcium-fructoborate record would need its own review.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Evidence suggests modest, formulation-dependent effects for common-cold outcomes; heterogeneity across preparations is substantial. The 2014 Cochrane review pooled 24 trials across Echinacea species and plant parts, including seven trials of Echinacea purpurea aerial-part preparations, so the registry-projected aerial, herb and purpurea root-extract preparation names are family-level joins. Species and plant part do not establish a studied dose or a product-specific effect. Dr. Pham's signed ruling of 2026-10-28: no general Echinacea prevention or treatment credit; a weak benefit from particular preparations remains possible and is not excluded. In the 2014 Cochrane review the 12 prevention comparisons were each non-significant (individual trials showed consistently positive but non-significant trends; a post hoc pooling suggested a 10-20% relative risk reduction), and 1 of 7 treatment trials shortened colds; this is not uniformly negative evidence.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: The best indexed pooled evidence remains the 2014 systematic review/meta-analysis (PMID 24554461), which found mixed but directionally favorable results for prevention or treatment of the common cold depending on product and regimen. Echinacea should therefore remain product-sensitive rather than presented as uniformly effective.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence for diindolylmethane is early, material-specific and confined to clinical populations. Both randomized trials used BioResponse DIM (BR-DIM): 150 mg/day for 6 months in women with newly diagnosed low-grade cervical cytological abnormalities (PMID 22075942, 551 women analysed), where DIM was unlikely to affect cytology or HPV infection and the CIN2+ difference was not significant; and 150 mg twice daily for 12 months in women taking tamoxifen (PMID 28560655, n=130), whose primary endpoint was a urinary estrogen-metabolite ratio - a biomarker, not a patient-important outcome. Neither trial asks whether DIM does anything for the general hormone-balance use these products are sold for. Scope repair 2026-09-18: applicability is now restricted to the branded material the trials used, and indole-3-carbinol rows are excluded.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 22075942 (BJC 2012): pragmatic double-blind RCT, 150 mg/day DIM from BioResponse DIM vs placebo for 6 months; of 551 randomised women analysed, 9% on DIM and 12% on placebo had CIN2+ (RR 0.7, 95% CI 0.4-1.2) and the authors conclude DIM 'is unlikely to have an effect on cytology or HPV infection'. PMID 28560655 (BCRT 2017): 130 women on tamoxifen randomised to BR-DIM 150 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months; the 2/16alpha-OHE1 ratio and SHBG rose and breast density did not change, while plasma tamoxifen metabolites including endoxifen FELL versus placebo (P<0.001). That last finding is a drug-interaction signal and belongs to the interaction owner (ingredient_interaction_rules / curated_interactions), not to an efficacy direction here; it is logged as a handoff, not as a rule, because interaction severity is that owner's review.

limitations: The effect is trivial (g 0.15). No included study was at low risk of bias (66 high risk, 58 some concerns), and daily nitrate dose was not associated with effect size (meta-regression p=0.93).

Dr. Pham fifth ruling (2026-10-28): Evidence recognizes the verified beetroot/nitrate performance relationship without a nitrate label gate; Dose stays unassessable against a nitrate benchmark when nitrate content is unknown, and beetroot powder mass does not establish nitrate exposure.

The effect is small (g 0.15). backed_clinical_studies.notes: Whey-specific evidence (Dr. Pham 2026-10-28): the network meta-analysis PMID 42625626 (36 RCTs) gives whey versus placebo lean mass +1.24 kg (moderate certainty) with exploratory strength gains, in adults doing supervised resistance training. Credit attaches only when every declared protein source is a whey form (aliases); casein, milk protein, soy, pea and mixed protein sources do not inherit it, and the earlier mixed-protein review (28698222) is not whey-specific proof. A generic Protein macro or unspecified blend does not identify whey. The exploratory 30-35 g/day plateau is not a Dose benchmark. No weight-loss or fat-burning credit.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A 49-study meta-analysis in 1,863 healthy adults found protein supplementation modestly improved resistance-training gains in strength, fat-free mass, and muscle size, with no additional fat-free-mass gain above about 1.62 g/kg/day total protein intake (PMID: 28698222). A whey-specific synthesis in older adults found improved lower-body strength with resistance training, but no significant improvement in handgrip strength, physical performance, or most body-composition outcomes (PMID: 39303495).

backed_clinical_studies.notes: The cited berberine sources concern different interventions. PMID 18442638 is a small diabetes pilot with a randomized berberine-versus-metformin cohort and a separate add-on cohort; gastrointestinal adverse effects were frequent. PMID 27157250 instead synthesizes a multi-ingredient formula containing red yeast rice, berberine, policosanol, astaxanthin, coenzyme Q10 and folic acid; its effects cannot be assigned to isolated berberine. NCT04697186 concerns berberine plus amoxicillin and rabeprazole for Helicobacter pylori, not standalone supplement treatment. NCT03281096 registered post-colorectal-cancer adenoma prevention, but its brief regimen and arm-level schedule conflict; a universal daily exposure is not established by that registration. Registry phase or completion counts are not clinical efficacy.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 18442638 randomized 36 newly diagnosed type2 diabetes patients to berberine or metformin and separately studied 48 poorly controlled patients receiving add-on berberine; it does not establish universal clinical equivalence. PMID 27157250 pools a six-ingredient nutraceutical combination. The published NCT04697186 report (PMC10107123) concerns a complete antibiotic/PPI/berberine regimen. NCT03281096 lists1,000 participants but has no posted results in the inspected registry payload; its description says300mg daily while intervention arms specify300mg twice daily for3years. Resolve the source conflict before quantitative applicability; absence of posted registry results does not prove no publication exists.

key_endpoints: PMID 11498460: In 153 coronary-artery-disease patients with low HDL, simvastatin plus niacin changed lipid measures over 12 months; added antioxidants blunted the HDL response. This combination study does not isolate niacin efficacy.

PMID 15642562: A Coronary Drug Project analysis reports cardiovascular and mortality findings for niacin versus placebo in men with previous myocardial infarction, including extended follow-up. The full 8,341-person trial included multiple drug regimens, not only niacin.

PMID 9732910: In peripheral-vascular-disease patients, niacin lowered fibrinogen and LDL; changes were correlated. These are selected-population surrogate outcomes; the abstract does not establish dose or course.
PMID 25141367: An uncontrolled red-yeast-rice-led multi-ingredient pilot reported lipid changes in 16 analyzed participants. It cannot establish independent niacin efficacy.
backed_clinical_studies.notes: Niacin has strong lipid-modifying evidence at pharmacologic doses (1-3g/day). AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE found no incremental benefit when added to statin therapy, but standalone evidence from the Coronary Drug Project remains positive. Supplement doses (50-500mg) have less direct evidence. The cited combination, uncontrolled and selected disease-population studies require separate applicability review. Nicotinamide in HIV research is not equivalent to nicotinic-acid lipid efficacy.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: The retained PubMed sources concern lipid outcomes or secondary prevention: 11498460 (simvastatin-niacin combination), 15642562 (Coronary Drug Project post-MI analysis), 9732910 (peripheral vascular disease biomarkers), and 25141367 (uncontrolled multi-ingredient pilot). Excluded from niacin lipid-efficacy support: NCT01411436 is sorafenib postmarketing surveillance in hepatocellular carcinoma; NCT00619541 is sorafenib plus infusional 5-fluorouracil in hepatocellular carcinoma. NCT02961829 includes nicotinamide with antiretroviral therapy in HIV and does not establish nicotinic-acid lipid efficacy. These identifiers are retained for traceability, not counted as qualifying niacin studies.

key_endpoints: Human synthesis of seven clinical studies found lower total cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting blood sugar and increased HDL-C; LDL-C and HbA1c were not significantly improved. Twenty-seven preclinical studies were analyzed separately (PMID: 34538515).

Small randomized pilot in 16 ACE-inhibitor-treated hypertensive patients: systolic blood pressure and selected endothelial biomarkers improved with 4.5 g/day for 12 weeks; adjunctive population, not general cardiovascular-event prevention (PMID: 30544795).

In 73 HIV-infected adult women before HAART, 5g/day for 3 months increased serum antioxidant capacity; no between-group differences in immunological or virological markers were observed. Antioxidant capacity is a surrogate outcome (PMID: 25057105)

In 23 children aged 2-13 with nephrotic syndrome, medication plus 1g/day for 2 months produced within-group TC and LDL-C decreases of 116.33 and 94.14 mg/dL; the medication-only control also decreased by 69.87 and 61.13 mg/dL. These are not placebo-adjusted treatment effects (PMID: 12487756)
backed_clinical_studies.notes: Reviewed mixed clinical findings with preparation- and population-specific applicability. PMID 34538515 separates seven human clinical studies from 27 preclinical studies and reports null LDL-C/HbA1c findings alongside positive metabolic biomarkers. PMID 35988871 reports eight direct Spirulina-placebo studies/420 participants, 6–16 weeks, with a small LDL-C reduction and VERY LOW certainty. Its 131-trial/13062-participant total spans eleven nutraceuticals and is not a Spirulina study count. Later lipid review PMID 37263369 supports a lipid biomarker signal, not longevity or cardiovascular-event prevention; overlapping reviews must not be summed as independent trials. The HIV trial reports an antioxidant surrogate without between-group immunological/virological benefit; the pediatric nephrotic-syndrome study reports adjunctive within-group changes. No immune protection, longevity or ordinary-dose muscle-recovery claim is established. The existing conservative rct_single/tier_2 scoring representation is retained; source summaries do not automatically upgrade numerical study-type credit. The HIV and pediatric adjunctive studies are not evidence of general longevity benefit.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: NCT04988347: 45 screened/43 randomized in linked PMID38401078, 1.6 g/day for two months after PPI withdrawal; dyspeptic rebound improved, reflux did not. NCT01752972: nonrandomized open-label arsenic-exposure study, 30 enrolled, no posted results. NCT05016557: randomized basic-science protein-synthesis study, 36 enrolled, 25 g protein bolus, no posted results or linked publication; not ordinary-dose clinical muscle-recovery evidence.

key_endpoints: LAPIBSS tested a two-strain L. acidophilus mixture in 80 adults at 10 billion total CFU/day (two 5-billion capsules) for 8 weeks. Primary abdominal pain result was null; secondary flatus and composite scores improved. The cited communication reviews that trial, not independent single-strain efficacy (PMID: 32538776)

An eight-strain formulation at 10 billion total CFU/day randomized 350 children, with 313 in intention-to-treat analysis. Primary antibiotic-associated diarrhea was null (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.49-1.33); secondary all-cause diarrhea decreased (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.94). Combination-only findings (PMID: 35727573)
A six-species formulation in 49 IBS patients improved primary symptom relief (68% versus 37.5% placebo); this formula result cannot be assigned to acidophilus alone (PMID: 23829297)

A meta-analysis of 12 heterogeneous probiotic trials in 744 children reported shorter diarrhea duration (SMD -0.74). The pooled intervention is probiotics, not isolated acidophilus efficacy (PMID: 35070839)
backed_clinical_studies.notes: REFERENCE CONTEXT ONLY: these IBS and diarrhea sources assess two-strain, multispecies or heterogeneous pooled probiotic interventions. They cannot establish efficacy for arbitrary L. acidophilus labels or another exact strain. LAPIBSS did not improve primary abdominal pain; secondary findings are not single-strain evidence. The pediatric eight-strain trial had a null primary AAD endpoint and a positive secondary all-cause-diarrhea result. Exact-strain evidence remains owned by clinically_relevant_strains.json. No generic-species numerical clinical credit is authorized; this bounded review does not establish absence of acidophilus human evidence.

LIMITATIONS CARRIED DELIBERATELY, verified against the sources on 2026-09-18: the larger synthesis reports substantial heterogeneity (LDL-C I2 = 77%, triglycerides I2 = 62%) and its own PREDICTION INTERVALS CROSS NULL for both (LDL-C -48.29 to 18.13; triglycerides -73.47 to 28.77), meaning a future trial could plausibly show no benefit; only hs-CRP is homogeneous (I2 = 0%). The two syntheses are NOT independent replications - 9 RCTs searched to April 2021 and 5 RCTs searched to December 2022 on the same ingredient and outcomes will substantially overlap - so they are recorded as agreeing, not as confirming one another. The endpoints are physiological and clinical biomarkers, not demonstrated reductions in cardiovascular events. The 500 mg/day floor is supported by the dose range the 9-RCT synthesis itself reports across its included trials, not by one branded preparation; the measured catalog label median is 120 mg/day, so most amla products stay out. SCORING HELD 2026-09-18 (owner decision, direction NOT changed): the record stays positive_weak and keeps its 500-1500 mg/day dose context, but it is held at reference tier so it contributes no points. Reason: the existing primary-mass floor overstates positive_weak evidence here. Measured on DSLD 232044 (Capros amla extract 500 mg as the only scorable active), the chain is primary floor 14.0 x positive_weak 0.85 = 11.9 raw, then rescaled by the generic_botanical_branded archetype reference (11.9 / 18.0 x 20) = 13.2 of 20 - for overlapping syntheses with LDL-C and triglyceride prediction intervals crossing null and biomarker rather than patient-important endpoints. The 2016 Cochrane update reports that Harpagophytum procumbens seems to reduce non-specific low back pain more than placebo, with evidence of moderate quality at best. The exposure it describes is HARPAGOSIDE, not extract mass, and the primary trials state the figures: PMID 10101629 gave Harpagophytum extract WS 1531 at 600 and 1200 mg containing 50 and 100 mg of harpagoside, and PMID 12509627 gave Doloteffin containing 60 mg of harpagoside daily. Measured against the catalog on 2026-09-18: exactly 1 of 25 products states harpagoside on its label (standardised to 1.5% of a 700 mg extract, about 10.5 mg/day) - roughly five times BELOW the lowest studied harpagoside dose. No catalog product currently establishes the studied exposure, so this entry is held at reference tier and contributes no evidence points. No extract-milligram to harpagoside conversion is proposed, and no harpagoside floor is encoded, because the applicability owner compares extract mass and a numeric marker floor there would wrongly pass a 700 mg extract against a 50 mg marker threshold. That senna works as a laxative is not in dispute: PMID 33767108 grades the short- and long-term efficacy of senna as good (grade A) evidence supporting first-line use for chronic constipation. IMPORTANT LINEAGE CORRECTION 2026-09-18: an earlier draft of this entry presented PMID 35943487 as a second independent grade-A review. It is not - it states in its own abstract that it is 'a synopsis of an updated systematic review the authors conducted', so it shares an evidence base with the first and may not be counted as independent confirmation. PMID 29885259 IS independent, but it is modest: 7 RCTs and 444 patients in long-term care, senna superior to or as effective as other laxatives, with the authors noting short trial durations and low quality in some included trials. The applicability problem is potency, not efficacy: the evidence is characterised by SENNOSIDE exposure while catalog labels state senna leaf extract mass, and no source establishes an extract-milligram equivalence. Measured 2026-09-18: 0 of 15 catalog products state sennosides on the label, so nothing establishes the studied exposure and this entry contributes no evidence points. SAFETY IS A SEPARATE OWNER: senna is a stimulant laxative with abdominal pain, cramping, bloating, diarrhoea and nausea reported as common adverse events and dependence and electrolyte concerns on chronic use; those are routed to the safety owner and do not reduce the efficacy direction recorded here.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 33767108 (Am J Gastroenterol 2021): 'We found good evidence to recommend polyethylene glycol or senna as first-line laxatives'. PMID 35943487 (J Am Assoc Nurse Pract 2022) is a synopsis of the authors' own updated systematic review of 41 randomized trials of at least 4 weeks, reaching the same grade A conclusion - the same evidence base restated, not a replication. PMID 29885259 (2018) is an independent systematic review of 7 RCTs and 444 long-term-care patients in which senna was superior to or as effective as other laxatives, with the authors cautioning that short durations and variable quality leave long-term efficacy and safety inconclusive.
backed_clinical_studies.effect_direction_rationale: positive_strong as a DESCRIPTION of the laxative literature - one grade A systematic review plus an independent long-term-care review agreeing - held at reference tier so it earns nothing, because no catalog label establishes the sennoside exposure the evidence is characterised by. Confidence lowered from high to medium on 2026-09-18 after verifying that PMID 35943487 is the authors' own synopsis rather than a second independent grade-A review. study_type=reference; evidence_level=reference; total_enrollment omitted because no synthesis states a pooled participant total.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: REVIEWED NULL, not unreviewed. The decisive source is a 598-participant double-blind placebo-controlled trial across 99 UK primary care centres: 2 g/day of D-mannose powder for 6 months did not reduce the proportion of women with recurrent UTI who went on to contact ambulatory care with a clinically suspected UTI (51.0% vs 55.7%; risk difference -5%, 95% CI -13% to 3%), with no significant difference in any secondary outcome, and the authors conclude it should not be recommended for prophylaxis in this group. A 2025 meta-analysis of 6 RCTs and 1,167 participants agrees (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.29-1.15). Earlier favourable syntheses rest on open-label and secondary-care studies that the placebo-controlled trial supersedes. Under the 2026-09-18 owner decision a null direction contributes zero affirmative efficacy credit: this record exists so the review state is known and explainable, not to add or subtract points.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: REVIEWED NULL, not unreviewed. Three single-ingredient randomized trials in healthy trained men found no testosterone benefit: 6 g/day for 12 weeks in resistance-trained men (no change in total or free testosterone), 3 g/day in a placebo-controlled crossover in male climbers (no effect on testosterone, calculated free testosterone or luteinizing hormone), and 6 g/day for 14 days in boxers under simulated altitude (no effect on testosterone, cortisol or haematological responses). A fourth trial reporting benefit gave D-aspartic acid together with ubiquinol and zinc to men attending an infertility clinic; a three-component combination in a clinical population may not lend its direction to this ingredient. Under the 2026-09-18 owner decision a null direction contributes zero affirmative efficacy credit. An additional 24-participant resistance-training trial (PMID 25844073) found no testosterone effect at 3 g/day for 14 days, but reduced total/free testosterone at 6 g/day. The aggregate determination retains zero affirmative efficacy credit; null trials and this negative biomarker result are distinguished, and training harm is not established.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 28841667 (PLoS One 2017): randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 22 resistance-trained men, 6 g/day for 12 weeks - no change in basal total or free testosterone; estradiol fell 16%. PMID 29893592 (IJSNEM 2019): single-blinded placebo-controlled crossover, 16 male climbers, 3 g/day for 2 weeks - no significant effect on testosterone, calculated free testosterone or luteinizing hormone. PMID 38201906 (Nutrients 2023): 16 male boxers, 6 g/day for 14 days with normobaric hypoxia - no significant effect on testosterone, cortisol or haematology. PMID 25844073 (JISSN 2015): 24 resistance-trained men randomized to placebo, 3 or 6 g/day for 14 days; 3 g/day had no significant testosterone effect, while 6 g/day reduced total and free testosterone; effects on strength/hypertrophy remain unknown.
backed_clinical_studies.effect_direction_rationale: No affirmative testosterone/training benefit in the reviewed trained-men trials. Three trials are null; PMID 25844073 is null at 3 g/day and negative for testosterone at 6 g/day after 14 days. This aggregate null/no-benefit determination does not erase the negative per-study result or establish training harm. Confidence remains medium because trials are small (16-24 participants). total_enrollment=24 denotes the largest single trial, not a sum.
